$doc: The story behind a rivalry or trophy game, shown in the game's details under 'The rivalry, deep cut'. Keyed by the two teams' logo ids, sorted and joined with '|' (the same key as the trophy photos). Only facts that were checked against more than one source are written here, with the sources listed; a disputed point says it is disputed. All-time records are NOT stored: they change every season, so the details already show them from the live series data. Add a rivalry by adding an entry here, nothing else.

oklahoma|texas.title: Red River Rivalry
oklahoma|texas.summary: Texas and Oklahoma meet at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas, in the middle of the State Fair of Texas, rather than on either campus.
origin: The first game was in 1900, a 28–2 Texas win.
Since 1932 the game has been played at the Cotton Bowl inside Fair Park in Dallas, during the State Fair of Texas, so it is a neutral-site game even though neither school is in Dallas.

trophy.name: Golden Hat
trophy.text: The State Fair of Texas donated the trophy in 1941, first as a bronze hat. When it was reworked in the 1970s it came out gold, and it has been the Golden Hat since.

moments.text: Oklahoma set the series records for most points and widest margin of victory.

alabama|auburn.title: The Iron Bowl
alabama|auburn.summary: Alabama and Auburn play for the state's bragging rights, and for decades there was no game at all.
origin: The first game was in Birmingham in 1893: Auburn 32, Alabama 22.

After the 1907 game the schools stopped playing over a disagreement, and the series did not resume until 1948. Accounts differ on who gave way: one says the Alabama legislature pushed the schools back together by threatening funding, another says Auburn asked for the game in 1944 and Alabama refused.

moments.title: The Kick Six
moments.text: Tied 28–28, No. 1 Alabama tried a 57-yard field goal with one second left. It fell short, and Auburn's Chris Davis, who usually returned punts and was standing deep in the end zone for exactly this, ran it back 109 yards for a 34–28 win. No. 4 Auburn went on to the SEC Championship Game.

sources.label: Oral history of the Kick Six, Awful Announcing

michigan|minnesota.title: The Little Brown Jug
michigan|minnesota.summary: One of college football's best-known rivalry trophies began as a water jug and a coach's suspicion.
origin: In 1903 Michigan coach Fielding Yost reportedly worried Minnesota might tamper with the team's water, so a student manager bought a jug for the visit. It cost 30 cents.

The game ended 6–6. Michigan left the jug behind, and a Minnesota custodian, Oscar Munson, found it in the visitors' locker room. Minnesota athletic director Louis "Doc" Cooke kept it and made it a trophy.
The trophy series is usually dated from 1909, when Cooke and Yost agreed the winner would keep the jug.

trophy.name: Little Brown Jug
trophy.text: A plain earthenware jug, painted with the score of each game. Several famous details are disputed: that Yost wrote to demand it back, and even whether the jug at the 1903 game was brown (one account says white). The name may come from an 1869 song, 'Little Brown Jug,' by Joseph Winner.

sources.label: The origins of the Little Brown Jug, Bentley Historical Library
A brief history of the Little Brown Jug, Minnesota Daily

army|navy.title: Army–Navy Game
army|navy.summary: The service academies' game, with the Commander-in-Chief's Trophy at stake in a three-way series.
origin: The first game was on November 29, 1890, at West Point: Navy 24, Army 0.
The teams have played every year since 1930; they have missed ten years in all.

trophy.name: Commander-in-Chief's Trophy
trophy.text: Since 1972 the trophy has gone to the winner of the season-long series among Army, Navy and Air Force. Army–Navy is the last of the three games.
